en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Forfeiture (Nissaggiyakaṇḍa)
The Chapter on the Groups:
29. The Training Rule on Perilous Places.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, having completed their rains retreat, the monks were dwelling in forest lodgings.
Robbers of the month of Kattika,
thinking, "We have gained a profit," began to harass them.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, having given a discourse on the Dhamma with regard to this cause and this occasion, addressed the bhikkhus:
“I allow you, bhikkhus, for one dwelling in forest dwellings, to leave behind one of the three robes inside an inhabited area.”
Now at that time, the monks— thinking, “It has been permitted by the Blessed One for one dwelling in forest lodgings to leave one of the three robes behind in an inhabited area”—
left one of the three robes behind in an inhabited area and stayed apart from it for more than four nights.
Those robes were lost, ruined, burnt, or gnawed by rats;
the bhikkhus became poorly clad and wore coarse robes.
The bhikkhus said this:
“Friends, why are you poorly clad and wearing coarse robes?
Then those monks informed the monks of this matter.
Those monks who were few in desires... [and so on]... they criticized, complained, and spread it about:
“How indeed can these monks, having deposited one of their three robes within an inhabited area, dwell apart from it for more than four nights?
Then those monks, having rebuked them in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One. … [The Buddha asked:
“Is it true, monks, that monks, having deposited one of their three robes within an inhabited area, dwell apart from it for more than four nights?”
“It is true, Blessed One,” they replied.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:

“… How can those foolish men, monks, having deposited one of their three robes within an inhabited area, dwell apart from it for more than four nights? This is not suitable, monks, this is not fitting…” [and so on].
“Monks, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence … [as before] … And so,
monks, you should recite this training rule: ‘Now,
having entered the rains residence on the full moon of Kattika, as for those forest lodgings that are considered risky— ’”
While dwelling in such perilous lodgings, a bhikkhu who so desires may,
if there is some reason for him to be separated from it, deposit one of his three robes within an inhabited area.

That bhikkhu may be separated from that robe for at most four nights. If he should remain separated from it longer than that, except by the authorization of the Saṅgha, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
“Now, as for ‘having completed the rains residence’,” this refers to those who have finished the rains retreat.
"The full moon of Kattika" refers to the Kattika festival (the full moon of the month of Kattika).
"Those forest lodgings," however, [are as follows].
A forest dwelling (āraññaka) means a resting place that is at least five hundred bow-lengths distant from the nearest village.
It is called "dangerous" (sāsaṅka).

In a monastery or its vicinity, the place where thieves have encamped is seen; the place where they have eaten is seen; the place where they have stood is seen; the place where they have sat is seen; the place where they have lain down is seen.
A monastery or its vicinity is called "dangerous" when people are seen there who have been killed by thieves, robbed, or beaten.
“A bhikkhu dwelling in such resting places” means a bhikkhu dwelling in resting places of this kind.
“Desiring” means...
"Desiring":
one of the three robes—
either the outer cloak (saṅghāṭi), the upper robe (uttarāsaṅga), or the inner robe (antaravāsaka).
"Should place it within a house" means he should place it in the surrounding village where he goes for alms.
"And there might be some reason for that bhikkhu to be separated from that robe-cloth."
There may be a reason; there may be something to be done.
"That bhikkhu may be separated from that robe for a maximum of six nights" means he may be separated from it for up to six nights.
"Except by the consent of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus" means setting aside the consent of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
"If she should stay apart from him beyond that" means...
At the rising of the sun on the seventh day, it becomes subject to forfeiture.
It is to be forfeited to the Saṅgha, or to a group, or to an individual.
And thus, monks, should it be forfeited:
…pe… “Venerable sir, this robe-cloth of mine has been separated from me for more than four nights, except by the consent of the Saṅgha; it is to be relinquished.
I relinquish it to the Saṅgha. …pe…
"Should give," ... "should give," ... "I give to the Venerable One."

If he stays apart for more than six nights, perceiving it as more than six nights, except by the consent of the Saṅgha, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya pācittiya).
If he stays apart for more than six nights, being in doubt, except by the consent of the Saṅgha, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.
If he stays apart for more than six nights, perceiving it as less than six nights, except by the consent of the Saṅgha, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.
Perceiving it as relinquished when it has not been relinquished ...
perceiving it as distributed when it has not been distributed ...
perceiving it as lost when it is not lost ...
If he stays apart from his robe while it is not lost, yet perceives it as lost;
or while it is not burnt, yet perceives it as burnt;
or while it has not been stolen, yet perceives it as stolen—unless there is permission from the Saṅgha of monks, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If one uses a robe that ought to be relinquished without having relinquished it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If it is less than twelve nights and one perceives it as more, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is less than twelve nights and one is doubtful, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is less than four nights and he perceives it as less,
there is no offense.
There is no offense if he stays apart for four nights.
He dwells apart for less than four nights;
having dwelt apart for four nights, he returns to the village boundary, stays there, and then departs;
within the four nights, he relinquishes it, gives it away, it is lost, it is destroyed, it is burned, they take it by force, or they take it on trust.
By means of the consent of the bhikkhus,
for one who is insane,
and for the first offender.
The ninth training rule concerning suspicion is finished.
